identity.title: Orthopnea: dyspnea lying flat relieved by sitting up / number of pillows

technique.how: Ask whether breathlessness starts or worsens within minutes of lying flat and is relieved by sitting up, and how many pillows or what head elevation is needed to sleep; distinguish from habitual pillow use for comfort or reflux. Ask about bendopnea (dyspnea within ~30 s of bending forward) as a related filling-pressure symptom.
technique.prerequisites: Reliable historian or collateral; clarify that the pillows are for breathing rather than comfort or GERD.

interpretation.positive_finding: True orthopnea reflects raised left-sided filling pressure on recumbency and is relatively specific for heart failure (specificity ~89% in primary care), though it also occurs in severe COPD, bilateral diaphragm weakness, massive ascites/obesity and large pericardial effusion.
interpretation.negative_finding: Absence of orthopnea is common in heart failure (sensitivity roughly 0.2-0.8 across ED studies) and does not exclude it.
interpretation.pitfalls: Patients often report pillow number without connecting it to dyspnea; chronic HF patients on diuretics may lose orthopnea despite elevated wedge pressure. Platypnea (worse upright) points to shunt or hepatopulmonary syndrome instead.
interpretation.changes_what: Orthopnea shifts undifferentiated dyspnea toward acute HF/volume overload and prompts JVP, S3, BNP or lung POCUS; absence should not remove HF from the differential.

sources.citation: Mant J, Doust J, Roalfe A, et al. Systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis of diagnosis of heart failure, with modelling of implications of different diagnostic strategies in primary care. Health Technol Assess 2009;13(32):1-207.
Signs and symptoms in adult patients with acute dyspnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Eur J Emerg Med 2018;25(1):3-11 (author list not retrievable via abstract tool; confirmed by PMID/DOI).
Wang CS, FitzGerald JM, Schulzer M, Mak E, Ayas NT. Does this dyspneic patient in the emergency department have congestive heart failure? JAMA 2005;294(15):1944-56.
Mueller C, Frana B, Scholer A, Laule-Kilian K, Perruchoud AP. Emergency diagnosis of congestive heart failure: impact of signs and symptoms. Can J Cardiol 2005;21(11):921-4.

estimates.target_condition: Heart failure (new diagnosis) in primary care
estimates.population: Patients with suspected heart failure in primary care; IPD meta-analysis of 9 studies
estimates.reference_standard: Echocardiography / expert panel per included studies
estimates.quote: orthopnoea (89%), oedema (72%), elevated jugular venous pressure (70%), cardiomegaly (85%), added heart sounds (99%), lung crepitations (81%)

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not use absence of orthopnea to exclude heart failure or tamponade, and do not attribute orthopnea to HF without examining for effusion, ascites or neuromuscular weakness.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Orthopnea with inability to lie flat at all plus hypotension or hypoxemia indicates flash pulmonary edema or tamponade and needs immediate assessment.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Symptom elicitation varies with how the question is phrased; pillow count alone is unreliable.

extraction_notes: Wang 2005 RCE reports orthopnea LR+ ~2.2 (CI ~1.2-3.9) in its evidence table, but the JAMA table is not accessible through the abstract tool, so it is not entered as an estimate. The Eur J Emerg Med 2018 review gives only ranges for orthopnea (sensitivity 0.2-0.76, specificity 0.49-0.92) without a pooled point estimate, so no estimate is recorded from it. Mueller 2005 (ED, n=452) did not report an orthopnea OR in the abstract. Only Mant 2009 specificity (89%) is abstract-visible, hence partially_quantified; sensitivity is null. Searches for primary hemodynamic studies (Chakko 1991, Stevenson 1989) found no orthopnea-specific numbers in abstracts.
